#260. Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”

#256. GTA 6 is giving Carly Rae Jepsens Run Away With Me a second life

Grand Theft Auto VI is a massive pop culture event that is affecting a whole lot of people from a whole lot of different angles. Arguably, few are benefiting more from the game's launch last week than Carly Rae Jepsen.

The Canadian pop star broke big worldwide with "Call Me Maybe" in 2012 and has followed up with an extremely respectable career that includes a devoted fanbase and eight studio albums, including the recently released Day & Night. However, one of her most beloved (and slightly less-well-known) songs is blowing up on streaming for the first time in a decade thanks to its inclusion in GTA 6, per Billboard Canada.

That would be "Run Away With Me," the opening track to Jepsen's highly acclaimed 2015 record Emotion. Aside from being featured on GTA 6's in-game radio station Flash FM, "Run Away With Me" also soundtracks an important early-game mission. According to Billboard and an X account called Carly Rae Jepsen Charts, the song was streamed more than 100,000 times on both Saturday and Sunday, its two biggest individual streaming days since the song was new.

To be clear, this is not necessarily a case of GTA breathing life into an obscure old song. "Run Away With Me" made a small splash on music charts in Canada and a handful of other territories back in 2015, and was a critical darling both at the time and now. But the GTA bump is clearly very real, nonetheless.

Warning: The following section contains spoilers for an early mission in GTA 6.

If you're curious as to the specific context in which "Run Away With Me" and its iconic distorted saxophone riff are used in GTA 6, allow me to explain. During the game's first story chapter, players will run into a mission called "Day Release" that involves protagonists Jason and Lucia going to a party on an expensive yacht. Lucia's parole ankle monitor is temporarily disabled for this mission, and the whole idea is that she and Jason get to have a fun day of rich people debauchery together for the first time since she got out of prison.

A few minutes into the mission, Jason and Lucia are invited to ride jet skis with the host of the yacht party, and this is where the "Run Away With Me" needle-drop happens. As the two lovers speed around the waters of a fictional Miami stand-in, Jepsen's catchy chorus reverberates throughout the action. The best part is that the mission keeps going and includes several little gameplay vignettes, most of which are scored by a longer remix of the song provided by Overmono and Pegassi.

What makes this great for those who enjoy both GTA and Carly Rae Jepsen is that the song isn't used just because it's good. It also perfectly evokes the excitement of the early stages of being in love and sonically fits the high-speed action during the mission.

Needless to say, it's been stuck in my head ever since I played the mission a few days ago. I hope it gets there for you, too. #255. Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice

Ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and said he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”

For the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

#254. Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy

According to a study by the Körber Foundation, a growing number of Germans now oppose providing military aid to Ukraine. The majority also believes that Germany should take a neutral position between the US and China.

For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

#253. Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization

Understanding how NaaS architectures offer a flexible solution to enterprise network modernization efforts.

Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.

As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study.

This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.

AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.

AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.

AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.

NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.

Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations.

#250. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#249. Google filed a patent application for an AI TV channel starring you

Ever since Google introduced its Veo 3 AI video model in March 2025, AI-generated video has started appearing in social feeds, ads, and even movies on free streaming services.

Now, Google has sketched out how AI could make the person watching TV the star of their own show. In a patent application published Nov. 19, the company describes a feature called "My Channel," which would use a viewer's watch history to generate videos for them. In one version, the system could use the viewer's likeness and voice to cast them as the lead of their very own TV show.

Patsnap, the database that hosts the filing, offers an AI-generated "technical title" that sums up the idea as a way of "enhancing user engagement."

The patent-tracking site Patentlyze first spotted the filing and shared it with 404 Media, which covered it on Nov. 23. Patent records show that Google filed the application on May 13, 2025, but the company has yet to announce a product.

One drawing in the application shows a TV menu called "John's Channel," with a crime comedy, a rom-com, a sci-fi adventure, and an action thriller. In a sample prompt, the filing tells the AI to make a video where "the user will play the protagonist." Another example takes that a step further. If a cricket fan has been watching clips about a particular player, the AI could put them in a scene with that player or show them "cheering for India in the stands." New videos could be made on request or on a schedule, such as once a week or once a month. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

To work out what to make, the system could look at the titles and genres a person watches and how long they watch them. It could also factor in the viewer's age group, the device's language setting, or its location. Those details would go into instructions for the AI about what kinds of stories to make. The application also describes an "advertising stitcher" that would insert ads into the finished video before it plays. Because even a show with an audience of one needs some sort of commercial break.

There are pieces of this idea in Google products already. Google TV Freeplay, for example, offers hundreds of free, ad-supported channels, and Google Photos can turn a picture someone selects into a short video.

Google's filing describes using photos or videos to create a digital likeness of the viewer. In one version, a TV assistant could send audio from voice commands to a server, where it could be stored "in association with the user." The system could then "synthesize the voice of the user for the dialogue of a protagonist."

The filing says viewers may have some say in what gets collected and "how that information is used." It leaves open whether someone could keep using voice commands to control the TV while opting out of having those recordings used to make a show, though.

For now, "My Channel" is still just an idea on paper. A patent examiner reportedly rejected Google's application, according to Patentlyze, for unknown reasons, and Google hasn't announced plans to launch it. The company can still seek to revise its claims or appeal. Mashable has reached out to Google for a comment.

#248. Amazon fights Delivery Protection Act by putting stickers on its packages

Amazon now uses its packages for political purposes.

Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill.

This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for New Yorkers.”

Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries.

Amazon previously sent mailers to NYC residents regarding a new headquarters (which was subsequently scrapped), but political messaging on packages is unprecedented for Amazon, which hasn’t used its delivery boxes to lobby for political causes before.

Last week, Amazon made another uncharacteristic move by showing NYC shoppers a homepage banner ad—which I see when logging in to Amazon as of this writing—and an in-app pop-up that also urges opposition to the bill. The banner and pop-up include a link to a blog where Amazon says the law would force it to consider moving operations outside of NYC and lead to “slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, however, support the bill.

By using its packages, website, and app to advocate against the bill, Amazon hopes to leverage its large customer base to push a political ideal. This raises concerns about whether it’s presenting the debate fairly, the appropriateness of using an e-commerce platform for political purposes, and whether we’ll see more political messaging while shopping with Amazon or other companies in the future.

As it stands, some shoppers are already put off by Amazon’s lobbying.

“Something about this just feels off to me,” a Reddit user who apparently received a package with the sticker wrote.

In a statement to CNBC last week, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the company is using the homepage and in-app messages to be “transparent with our customers” about what the proposed law “would cause them if it passes as written.”

As of Friday, Amazon shoppers had sent over 60,000 emails to NYC Councilmembers opposing the bill, NBC New York reported.

The City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection will decide whether to advance the bill to the entire council. The date for that vote hasn’t been set yet.

#247. Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra may get a camera downgrade

Is the Galaxy S27 Ultra really going to be a big downgrade for Samsung fans? It could be, at least when it comes to its cameras.

Earlier this month, Mashable reported on recent leaks suggesting that the Samsung Galaxy S27 lineup wasn't going to get much of an upgrade compared to its predecessors. The Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra fared slightly better than the other models, according to the leaks. It appears the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra will get a main camera sensor upgrade, along with a better selfie camera and a 5x zoom lens.

However, new leaks suggest the device could also lose a few camera features.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

According to leaker Ice Universe, Samsung may be dropping the laser autofocus module from the Galaxy S27 Ultra. Laser autofocus, also known as laser AF, uses a dedicated sensor that helps the camera quickly lock focus on a subject. If the leak is accurate, the S27 Ultra would be the first Galaxy S Ultra model without laser autofocus since at least 2021, when Samsung released the Galaxy S21 Ultra.

The removal of laser autofocus appears to be connected to the new camera layout on the Galaxy S27 Ultra, which was also previously leaked by Ice Universe. The Galaxy S27 Ultra will reportedly move away from the vertical camera setup on the Galaxy S26 Ultra and have a horizontal camera bar instead. The new layout is reportedly the reason behind the removal of laser autofocus.

That's not the only potential downgrade, as PhoneArena points out. Other leaks have also pointed to the Galaxy S27 Ultra losing its 3x telephoto lens.

If these leaks pan out, will the Galaxy S27 Ultra have other new features to balance out the downgrades and still lure in current users looking to upgrade? We'll likely find out at Samsung Galaxy Unpacked early next year.

#246. Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees on Tuesday for violating the company’s code of conduct. During his first all-hands since returning to his role as CEO, Huang said he made some “very serious personal mistakes” and that’s why he submitted his resignation.

“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”

Huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.”

The CEO emphasized that Nvidia’s code of conduct, much of which he said he wrote himself, still governs how employees are expected to treat one another and is intended to “create an environment that’s safe for people.”

Huang told employees that violations of the code would not be tolerated. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor in.

Huang also pushed back against the notion that he had received preferential treatment because of his status in Silicon Valley. “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said. He rejected the suggestion that he was above the law or Nvidia’s code of conduct.

Later in the meeting, Huang addressed criticism of his notoriously intense management style, acknowledging that his behavior had at times negatively affected employees. While Huang maintained that the intensity he brings to his job elevates those around him, he conceded that he sometimes takes things too far.

“It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang said. The Nvidia CEO said he needed to figure out how to maintain his level of dedication to the company without hurting the people who work there.

“I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” Huang said. He said that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as monthly from people who work with him. The CEO added that he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and that he did not want to institute the practice companywide.

Nvidia board members accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal scrutiny.

While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remain concerned about his conduct and the board’s decision to reinstate him. Huang and Nvidia also continue to face legal and regulatory scrutiny. The board is continuing an investigation into whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers are expecting him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips.

During the all-hands meeting, Huang also sought to reassure women at Nvidia, describing himself as “one of our greatest advocates for creating an environment for women” and touting the company’s flexible work policies, which he said allow employees to simultaneously build their families and careers.

“If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” Huang said.

The CEO also argued that his brief absence had demonstrated Nvidia’s ability to operate without him. “I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute,” Huang said.

#245. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#244. What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is possible.

A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.

On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.

An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.

The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.

The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.

Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.

As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

#243. GTA 6 has a smut book club and a surprisingly long reading list

Stealing cars, robbing banks, and getting into shootouts are all familiar ways to spend an afternoon in Grand Theft Auto VI. Apparently, there's also time for a little bit of reading.

Rockstar stocked its fictional Florida with books, magazines, and comics that players can pick up and flip through. There's a fishing magazine, little libraries across Leonida with their own reading lists, advertisements for "romantasy" novels on the radio, and even a backyard book club. Here's where to find something to read, what flipping through the pages can unlock, and how to drop in on that aforementioned book club. (I know I want to.)

GTA 6 has 34 reading collectibles, according to Power Pyx. The game groups 27 under Magazines, Books & Comics and tracks another seven at roadside libraries called Book Swaps. There's war fiction, crime memoir, self-help, sci-fi, and adventure, along with comics and magazines about everything from bodybuilding to fishing.

The books in GTA 6 range from crime memoirs to war novels and self-help parodies, and players can read a short excerpt from each.

At Jason's house in Key Lento, Lethal by Design opens to six pages from Chapter 7, where a small-time crook recounts working for Liberty City’s Ancelotti crime family.

By Jason's bed, the World War II novel Ashes of Glory offers six pages in which Captain Liberty and his squad of convicts survive a mission and realize no one planned for them to get out alive.

There's even a military self-help parody called ORCA: A Whole Different Animal, in which a veteran turns his training into life advice and brags about waking up at 2 a.m. to carry a 350-pound log to work.

An issue of Body Copy also gives players a magazine to flip through, from a fitness influencer's morning routine to gym etiquette and places to meditate outdoors.

The game tucks reading material into everyday stops, too. There's a copy of self-help book Help Me Help You Help Me at the Starlet Motel's front desk, and the comics Ratface and Special Friends Force share a rack at a food mart in Vice City's La Perle neighborhood. A trailer in Port Gellhorn has something a little harder to classify, though Dicked Down Deep in Space certainly sounds like sci-fi.

Some of Leonida's books can be spotted from the road. The game features seven roadside libraries called Book Swaps, each holding a few pages from a different adventure novel. For example, down the street from Jason's house, a turtle-shaped bookcase on Dolphin Drive holds Killer Prom. On Vespucci Island, a miniature lighthouse contains Goodnight, Dollface, Goodnight. You'll also find a boat-shaped shelf by Lake Leonida in Ambrosia with Humanity vs Space and a coffin-shaped bookcase outside Capri's Halloween House with Badlands Revenge inside.

The collection doesn't stop there. Three more Book Swaps are scattered across Leonida, including The Wizard's Ruin: Loud Clap of the Night in Watson Bay, Thighlander: A Tale of True Scotsmen in Southside, and Outback Gas Junkie in Waning Sands. Once a book or magazine catches your eye, look for the Examine prompt. On PlayStation, R1 turns the page, L1 goes back, and Triangle displays the text. Square flips the publication over to show the back cover.

To log a Book Swap, take the book out and put it back. It counts whether you flip through the pages or immediately get back in the car.

Reading in GTA 6 can be a fun detour that leads to new locations and side quests.

At Jason's house, pick up the fishing magazine Off the Hook from the workbench in the shed. Turn to the fishing guide, and five spots appear on your map, including a stretch of water east of Key Lento where you can catch barracuda and a spot beneath the Draper Island bridge where you can fish for tarpon.

Reading can also prompt to a phone call. Outside Three Sheets Liquor, there's a flyer from a man named Kirk who's looking for a creature called the Skunk Ape. Read it to add Kirk to your in-game contacts, then call him at night to start a side quest that takes you looking for the creature near Pelican River.

The phone comes in handy with style magazines, too. Scanning them with the WAiNK app can unlock hairstyles, makeup, and tattoos, which count toward the game’s separate Discovered Styles checklist. And back at Jason's house, Insider Gaming found that flipping through books and magazines gives his Focus meter a boost. Focus lets players slow down time in combat, so a little reading can come in handy the next time Jason gets into a shootout.

Reading also counts toward 100 percent completion, according to Power Pyx. Players need any 30 of the 34 unique titles across Magazines, Books & Comics and Book Swaps. Both collections are under Progress → Collections → Exploration.

Some copies become inaccessible as the story moves on, so Chapter 1 is a good time to look around Jason's place.

And if you prefer reading in a group setting, don't worry. There's even a book club in GTA 6. In the Chapter 3 side mission "Climbing the Cellerichain," Lucia drops off a package for her friend Andy at a house in Waning Sands. When she knocks, someone calls her around to the backyard, where a group of women are discussing a seemingly steamy novel called Two Pricks in the Bush. Lucia can leave once she drops off the package, or she can stick around and give her opinion on the book.

TikTok user @scorpionlibrarian shared a clip of the encounter with the caption “They ended up kicking me out." One commenter asked, "Where can I sign up."

There's clearly a market for these "romantasy" novels in Vice City: During his playthrough, Mashable's tech reporter Alex Perry heard an ad for a smut novel on the in-game radio.

#242. Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more

Personalized pricing can mean unfair, and even biased, prices.

Each month, we’ll examine the biggest controversial changes to tech products: What changed, why it’s happening, how users are affected, and how companies can do better.

“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

“The goal of surveillance pricing is to infer the highest price that the customer is willing to pay, based on consumers’ personal data and other market data,” EPIC explains.

Instacart previously practiced surveillance pricing, also called personalized pricing. In 2025, Consumer Reports found that, “based on how much Instacart says the typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year.” Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.

Dynamic pricing, or surge pricing, differs from surveillance pricing in that, instead of relying on consumer data, it uses changing market trends, like supply and demand, inventory levels, and competitor pricing, to set prices.

While dynamic pricing may charge you more for an Uber ride when it’s very busy, surveillance pricing can feel less reasonable.

For instance, Target’s app was previously accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV if they bought it while standing inside a Target store. At the time, Target said that it would match lower prices presented by customers, but many customers wouldn’t think to look for pricing discrepancies. In another instance from 2012, Orbitz was found to more prominently feature expensive hotels to people using macOS. Companies often dispute whether their practices truly qualify as surveillance pricing. But these examples all reflect companies using data about their customers to influence the prices they show them.

ZipRecruiter was one of the first companies to leverage surveillance pricing as we think of it today. In 2018, its profits increased 84 percent by using surveillance pricing versus charging every customer $99. Surveillance pricing is still somewhat nascent, but its potential lucrativeness and the growing availability of user data suggest it may become more common.

Other technological advancements, including advanced machine-learning methods, have further facilitated the growth of personalized pricing.

In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said at least 250 companies used surveillance pricing.

According to a 2025 statement from then-FTC Chair Lina M. Khan, “retailers frequently use people’s personal information to set targeted, tailored prices for goods and services—from a person’s location and demographics, down to their mouse movements on a webpage.”

Surveillance pricing has become more widespread as food delivery platforms, rideshare services, rental housing providers, and other businesses have gained access to the technology and data needed to implement it. Third-party data brokers, advertising and analytics companies, and credit providers make it easy for organizations to get the information needed to build customer profiles. The growth of web browsing, the Internet of Things, and user tracking have created data-rich digital lives that are simple for retailers to analyze.

Additionally, the rise of e-commerce means even more customer data is available, which makes it easier to charge customers different prices than a physical store could.

Surveillance pricing makes it hard for shoppers to get the best, or even fair, prices and makes it difficult to assess the true value of products. There are also broader implications that go beyond how consumers feel about it.

A 2025 report from the American Economic Liberties Project, “Prohibiting Surveillance Prices and Wages” (PDF), says surveillance pricing relies on biased algorithms:

Algorithms often rely on data that reflect historical and ongoing biases, embedding these prejudices into wage- and price-setting systems and perpetuating them. For example, as studies of rideshare company platforms have shown, riders traveling to predominantly non-white neighborhoods are often charged higher prices,a pattern that mirrors historical residential segregation. And … college test-prep services have sometimes been priced over $1,000 more in zip codes with large Asian populations.

Dating app Tinder, for example, was previously reported to use surveillance pricing to charge older users more money for subscriptions. Tinder denied that it used social or demographic data for pricing, agreed to pay $60.5 million to settle a class-action lawsuit about the charge, and says it stopped charging older users more.

Surveillance pricing also incentivizes data collectors to gather increasingly detailed, potentially intrusive, consumer data, which could be used in harmful or exploitative ways.

As EPIC states: “Consumers are categorized by data brokers that identify or infer characteristics such as age, demographics, shopping habits, lifestyle, or economic status. Such personal data collected for commercial purposes also often ends up in the hands of third parties, including law enforcement agencies, and is used for unrelated purposes.”

Some critics of surveillance pricing argue for legislation that bans the practice or sets parameters about how and when it’s used. However, some argue that legislation could hurt consumers, since surveillance pricing can also show customers lower prices.

Barring legislation, there are things that companies can do to better serve shoppers in this regard. One approach is to disclose when they are using personalized pricing, similar to when Uber alerts users that surge pricing is in effect.

Speaking of surge pricing, prioritizing dynamic pricing over surveillance pricing would allow organizations to continue leveraging data and real-time market conditions to maximize revenue while reducing the risk of biased or unfair pricing.

Surveillance pricing often occurs surreptitiously, so consumers, lawmakers, and retailers will likely continue to be challenged by the practice. Consumers can strive to protect themselves somewhat by setting their own standards for what they pay when possible. For instance, when I buy a new TV, I have an idea of how much I am willing or able to spend before I start shopping. If the prices don’t come close to aligning with my needs, I reassess my options, which may include using an aging gadget longer.

Shoppers should no longer assume that “it costs what it costs.” By setting personal spending limits and deciding in advance what you’re willing to pay, you can avoid paying more for a gadget, app, or service than is fair.

#241. iRestore Elite Laser Hair Growth System Review: Husband-Approved

The Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.

I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.

However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand said science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.

Red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.

Red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.

Importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.)

The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.

The Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.

If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.

The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't plan to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.

During the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a big no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.

Within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while new growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.

The effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.

Rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.

In addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.

The supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.

The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.)

Ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," says Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.

As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite showed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

#240. GTA 6 chapter 1 is so good that Im afraid to move on to chapter 2

I've run into a very stupid problem with Grand Theft Auto VI, a game I love so far.

Namely, I'm having a surprisingly difficult time moving on from chapter 1 of the game's sprawling crime story. For a couple of real-life days now, I've been sitting on the edge of finishing GTA 6's opening stanza with very little motivation to move on. At the time of writing, I have literally one story mission left to go before the first chapter ends, and almost nothing of substance left to do otherwise.

But as much as I know I need to break through and see the rest of what GTA 6 has to offer, it's hard to resist the call to just live out Jason Duval's mundane daily routine for eternity.

Warning: There are some light spoilers for early parts of GTA 6's story in the following section.

For those who haven't played GTA 6 yet or are still in the early stages like me, chapter 1 follows Jason's meager existence as a sort of paid goon for Brian, a local boatyard owner who dabbles in drug trafficking on the side. The other protagonist, Lucia, gets out of prison partway through the chapter, but for most of it, she's not playable yet. Most of the story and side missions in chapter 1 focus on Jason doing little odd jobs that occasionally spiral into chaotic violence. He spends time with his girlfriend or buddies and otherwise just kind of chills when he's not doing all the crime stuff.

GTA 6 chapter 1 immediately establishes an endearingly ordinary routine for Jason, at least by action video game protagonist standards. Every in-game day I wake up, feed the pet snake, drink coffee, work out, drink a protein shake, and take a shower before heading out to do whatever it takes to get enough money to set up a nest egg for Jason and Lucia.

While there are some minor gameplay incentives to doing all of that, GTA 6 doesn't outright demand any of it from the player. I'm just doing it because it's a legitimately interesting loop, especially by the standards of big-budget mainstream games. I'm not just endlessly traversing between icons on a map and shooting some bad guys when I get to each one. I feel like an active participant in the everyday lives of two adults, which at the very least is novel for this type of game. It also helps that Brian is voiced by Stephen Root, so you spend most of chapter 1 being yelled at by Buck Strickland, and that's lovely.

I mean, most of my favorite missions so far have barely involved crime at all. The one where Jason and Lucia go to a bar after she gets out of prison is a remarkable virtual rendition of a romantic night out, while I've already lavished the Carly Rae Jepsen mission with praise on this website.

All of that is why I'm having such a hard time moving forward with the main story. I know in my heart that chapter 2 will likely introduce a new setting with new stakes, new mechanics, and an increased focus on crime. And all of that will probably be fantastic in its own right, but it won't be the same as the game I've loved up until now.

And if that's the feeling Rockstar intends to elicit in players when chapter 1 draws to a close, I would say they pulled it off. Maybe even a little too well. #238. 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia

Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day, rethinking his management style, and says that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday.

Here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it's been helping me a lot.”

On accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I'm a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I'm a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I'm above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won't be tolerated. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn't tolerated here.”

“If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won't be tolerated. But ‘it won't be tolerated’ does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I'm going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.”

On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I'll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.”

On succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I'm here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results and financial results.”

“I also didn't believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.”

“There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning, it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.”

On politics: “There [were] also rumors that apparently I'm back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.”

“It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country. … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.”

“Don't think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don't love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”
