#236. Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it's a big secret

“I would ask you to please reach out to Roscosmos directly.”

It was the most simple of questions. On Monday afternoon, during a NASA news conference about the International Space Station, Space News reporter Jeff Foust asked about an upcoming launch of a Russian spacecraft.

“It’s my understanding there’s another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress,” Foust said. “Can you confirm that, and give the date and time that will launch?”

This Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday. It is going to a space station co-operated by the US space agency. But no, NASA would not provide this basic information about the upcoming Progress launch.

“Regarding the Progress launch, I would ask you to please reach out to Roscosmos directly for any questions tied to that vehicle,” said the senior NASA official on the call, Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager for NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program.

Effectively, this is a “Go f- yourself” response from NASA. Roscosmos typically does not reply to Western media outlets, and everyone knows this.

So why is a bog-standard Progress launch suddenly a state secret? It seems to be a recent policy change, because, historically, NASA has televised every one of these cargo flights from Russia’s main spaceport in Baikonur, Kazakhstan. But there is no information about the upcoming launch on NASA’s television schedule for upcoming “live” events.

As recently as September, NASA provided live television coverage of Progress launches from Baikonur. It even issued a media advisory promising to update its broadcast schedule once Roscosmos provided launch details. Two months later, NASA officials apparently are unwilling to confirm that another Progress launch is taking place.

The question is whether this decision was made by NASA or was a request from Roscosmos, and, ultimately, whether any of this matters. We can make some educated guesses.

It is probably safe to surmise that the decision here was originally made by state-sponsored Russian space corporation Roscosmos. The company has not been advertising the preparation of the Progress spacecraft as it customarily does, some local sources say. Russian space reporter Anatoly Zak confirms that Roscosmos has “dramatically curtailed” its coverage of all launch campaigns in recent months. There is no mention of the launch on Roscosmos’ Telegram channel.

So why is Roscosmos doing this? There are some novel aspects of this flight. Among the cargo being brought to the space station is a robot that was created to assist spacewalkers during extravehicular activities. Operated by humans, the human-like “Teledroid” is designed to operate in a vacuum, exposed to radiation. Surely nothing will go wrong with this.

This is also the first launch of a Progress spacecraft since NASA and Roscosmos agreed that the leaky PrK module on board the space station would be decommissioned. Zak reports that, as a result, the Progress spacecraft will first dock to the Poisk module, where it will be unloaded. It will then be moved from there to the docking port attached to the PrK module to provide propulsion for the space station. Docked there, the ship’s propulsion system is better aligned with the station’s main axis.

But none of this likely is the cause of secrecy surrounding Tuesday’s Progress launch. Rather, more likely it is due to Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Ars reported earlier this year that, after a spaceport in northern Russia came under attack from drones on multiple occasions, the Russian government put a tighter lid on information about its launches from Plesetsk. It now seems likely that Russia has extended this secrecy policy to other missions at other spaceports.

For example, earlier this month, Russia launched a Soyuz rocket from the Vostochny Cosmodrome without publicly announcing its precise launch date and time beforehand. Roscosmos confirmed the mission only after liftoff, and independent observers had to rely on local government notices to determine when the launch would occur.

Through all of the geopolitical turmoil on Earth, NASA has sought to maintain a good working relationship with Russia. Most likely, then, NASA has gone along with Russia’s secrecy policy for this week’s cargo launch—absurd though it appears in a culture of transparency.

Nevertheless, this kind of secrecy would seemingly be untenable with a crewed launch involving NASA astronauts. The next test of this will come in March 2027, when the Soyuz MS-30 mission carrying three astronauts, including NASA’s Deniz Burnham, is due to lift off from Baikonur. We’ll be watching.

#235. Chinese official gets death sentence in spy case, report says

A Chinese official recruited while working abroad was paid more than a million yuan to leak secrets, state-affiliated media reported.

A Chinese court has sentenced a government official to death for spying for a foreign country, according to a report published Monday by a state-linked social media account.

The official was reportedly convicted of passing on secret information in exchange for payment.

The report was published on an online account run by Gold Wall Press, a publisher tied to the National Administration of State Secrets Protection.

The report named the man only as Ma. The AFP news agency called him a ministerial official, while Reuters described him as an administrative official in China's central apparatus.

According to the report, a foreign operative called "Kailin" recruited Ma while he worked overseas. Kailin first met him regularly on the pretext of learning Chinese. The talks then turned to politically sensitive topics.

A colleague of Kailin's later threatened to tell Chinese authorities about Ma's earlier disclosures unless he cooperated. Later, Ma signed an agreement committing him to confidentiality and loyalty. He received monthly payments and a laptop for sending and receiving intelligence, the report said.

Upon returning to China, Ma kept passing on information, sending more than 100 intelligence reports, 35 of them later deemed "top secret," the report said. He was allegedly paid over one million yuan ($150,000, €138,000).

The sentence also includes confiscation of all his personal property.

The report did not say when or where Ma was sentenced, or whether he had already been executed.

Chinese courts rarely publish details of state security cases, but the secrecy regulator and the Ministry of State Security have increasingly publicized them as a warning to officials not to become spies.

"This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call," the report said.

In recent years, the US CIA has published videos in Mandarin seeking informants in China's bureaucracy and military, which Beijing has called a "damning confession."

#234. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#233. How to find your old Spotify Wrapped playlists and revisit your past music eras

Music has a funny way of transporting you back to a specific moment in your life. Sometimes, all it takes is the opening notes of a song to bring back an entire summer, a person you haven't spoken to in years, or a version of yourself you barely recognize anymore.

And if you've been using Spotify for the better part of a decade, chances are you've inadvertently been keeping a musical diary.

Since Spotify Wrapped debuted in 2016, the streaming platform has compiled personalized playlists of users' most-played songs each year. Collectively, those playlists offer a fascinating snapshot of how your taste in music — and, perhaps, your life — has changed over time.

With Spotify Wrapped 2026 just around the corner, there's no better time to revisit your past musical eras. What were you listening to before the pandemic? Which songs got you through lockdown in 2020? (Thank you, "God's Menu" by Stray Kids.) And what happened to that artist you were completely obsessed with in 2018?

Here's how to find your old Spotify Wrapped playlists.

Even after the annual Wrapped experience disappears from the Spotify app, your personalized Top Songs playlists may still be accessible. The easiest way to find them is through Spotify's search function. You can do this on the mobile app, desktop app, or web player.

Type "Your Top Songs" followed by the year you're looking for (for example, "Your Top Songs 2020").

Filter your search results by Playlists, if necessary.

Look for the personalized playlist created by Spotify.

Once you've found it, tap the plus icon to save it to your library for easy access.

You can repeat this process for each year you'd like to revisit.

If you're having trouble finding a particular playlist, a Spotify moderator recommends trying a few different search queries. For example, if you're looking for your 2020 Wrapped playlist, try searching for "Wrapped 2020" or "year:2020" (without any spaces).

Keep in mind that not every old Wrapped playlist will necessarily be available. If you didn't listen to enough music on Spotify during a particular year, the platform may not have generated a personalized playlist for you. Older playlists can also be trickier to track down. And when browsing your search results, look for the "Spotify • Made for you" label to make sure you've found your own personalized playlist rather than someone else's with a similar name.

Unfortunately, revisiting your old Spotify Wrapped playlists isn't quite the same as revisiting your old Spotify Wrapped.

Spotify doesn't offer a permanent archive of its annual interactive Wrapped experiences. That means you generally can't go back and see how many minutes you listened, who your top five artists were, or what else Spotify told you about your listening habits.

Want to know which Sound Town Spotify assigned you in 2023? Or what your Listening Personality was in 2022? Unless you saved a screenshot, you may be out of luck.

As for this year's Wrapped, consider saving screenshots of your favorite slides when it arrives. Your future self might appreciate them.

If you've managed to track down several years' worth of Wrapped playlists, why not make an afternoon of it?

Listen to your oldest playlist and see how many songs you still know by heart. Compare your top songs from five years ago with the music you're listening to today. Look for the artists who've remained a constant in your life and the ones you'd almost forgotten existed. You could even create a new playlist combining your favorite songs from every year of Wrapped, essentially making your own decade-spanning musical retrospective.

Part of the fun is discovering the little things your memory has lost along the way. The song you used to listen to on your morning commute. The album that became the soundtrack to a new city. The artist you discovered through a friend you no longer talk to. Or that time you fell asleep on a five-hour flight with aespa's "Illusion" on repeat, inadvertently catapulting it to the top of your most-played songs of 2022. (Just me?)

We tend to think of Spotify Wrapped as a year-end ritual, something to share on social media and collectively obsess over for a few days in December. But revisiting those playlists years later gives them an entirely different kind of significance.

Years later, there's something lovely about being able to visit a former version of yourself simply by pressing play.

#232. States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

X says every Grok output is screened, but state AGs say Grok is still making CSAM.

On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.

“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”

Millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.

“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a press release.

States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.

Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”

“Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.

Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the company has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety said that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.

“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”

However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises users how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.

Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok users, states alleged.

Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”

In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”

“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”

It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”

As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.

“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.

Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users.

“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.

Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.

“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

#230. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#229. Why your smart TV keeps losing its Wi-Fi connection

A smart TV can drop Wi-Fi for several reasons, and most of them have little to do with the TV.

It's not uncommon for smart TVs to struggle with a Wi-Fi connection, even if it's been relatively smooth sailing for a while. Things change, furniture gets moved around, routers are upgraded, new TVs are purchased and old TVs are moved to another room. Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 tri-band routers bring faster data rates to the table, but Wi-Fi 4 (2.4GHz and 5GHz dual-band support) is still the most prevalent Wi-Fi standard in the US. For the most part, 5GHz and 2.4GHz are enough for the average household, though it's ideal for most smart TVs to use 5GHz for 4K streaming.

It's a little tougher for 5GHz Wi-Fi, however, which is faster than 2.4GHz but lacks range and struggles with passing through walls. Your router's features could be making things worse. Many routers use "band steering" when broadcasting Wi-Fi, a feature that combines bands under a single network name, switching your devices back and forth automatically. It sounds convenient. You want your device connected to the most stable band, but it can wreak havoc on your TV's Wi-Fi connection. Devices don't always get the right band, degrading your smart TV's connection stability and speed. For those with older smart TVs, the lack of compatibility could be hampering your connection as well. Older models may not support DFS channels and won't find networks using them.

Isolate the problem and figure out whether it's the TV or the network by connecting a phone or a laptop to the same Wi-Fi network. If it runs fine, the issue is probably with your smart TV. If not, check your router, gateway or your internet service first.

Next, check if there's a firmware or software waiting for installation in the TV's system settings. If there's an update available but your internet connection isn't working, check the model name on the manufacturer's website to try and flash an update via USB stick instead.

Restarting could also be an easy fix. Unplug your TV for two minutes and the router for about a minute. Plug the router back in and let it reconnect before messing with the TV. If the problem persists, go into the TV's settings and clear out the saved connections. On your router settings, turn off band steering and give each available band its own name so you can choose which band the TV will use such as 36, 40, 44, or 48 instead of Auto. If the TV keeps dropping on 5GHz, set the band to a fixed channel outside the DFS range.

Most smart TV's default to a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi signal to avoid losing connection with your router. This band can interfere with special Bluetooth remote features like voice command, so try turning off the Bluetooth-reliant features on your remote. If Bluetooth is critical for accessibility reasons, switch the TV to 5GHz, bring the router closer, or go the direct route with an Ethernet cable.

Several factors go into this, including signal strength, network congestion, router placement and the TV's capabilities. If the signal is strong, the obvious choice is 5GHz. Switch to 2.4GHz only if the TV is too far from the router to hold a steady connection with 5GHz.

Speed and crowding are typical issues in most homes because everybody has a device or ten that connects to the internet. A 4K stream needs a steady 20 Mbps (Netflix suggests 15 Mbps, but 20+ is preferable). 2.4GHz has a longer range and handles walls better, but it's slower and usually more congested because neighboring routers, microwaves and Bluetooth devices can all interfere with it. Once you've eliminated band steering and renamed your bands, try each one out. Use your TV's network status screen to make a signal strength comparison.

Consider a wired connection. A close router makes this option more feasible, so you don't have to run an Ethernet cable across ceilings and under baseboards. If there's just too much space and you can't shrink the gap between the router and TV, a mesh network is another viable alternative. Most mesh nodes have Ethernet ports, so you can place one near your TV and run an Ethernet cable from the mesh to the TV. Just make sure your mesh network has a strong connection.

#227. Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally

The Army said on Sunday that it would carry out the detonation on Wednesday.

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.

The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

In late March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions to safely dispose of the lead azide, according to a New York Times report. MuniRem uses a sulfur-based solution that reportedly breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, eliminating the need for detonation. The company had proposed spraying the inside of the earth-covered containers housing the barrels as well as the barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions.

But two months later, the Army canceled the contract without explanation. An Army contracting officer told MuniRem in an email at the time that the cancellation “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s plans, the Times reported. The company’s founder said MuniRem filed public records requests to get more information on why the contract was scrapped, but it has not received a response.

Now, the Army claims that the lead azide has only degraded further since March and that it cannot move the barrels or even open their lids without risking a catastrophic explosion. Further, it claims that winter temperatures in the coming days increase the risk of spontaneous detonation.

“As the temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in a court filing over the weekend. “If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment.”

The Army claims that the only choice now is between a controlled, mitigated explosion or an uncontrolled, unmitigated explosion. In court filings this weekend, government lawyers argued that the Army does not need the now-suspended EPA permit to move forward with the detonation, because the Army has determined that the lead azide poses an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

Last Thursday, Telle said that the delay until Monday was the “latest possible moment” for a controlled detonation before temperatures dropped dangerously low. But the military subsequently delayed the detonation again until Tuesday and then pushed it back to Wednesday.

In his social media post Monday, Trump said he thought carrying out the controlled detonation was the “proper course.” But he said he was making the decision the responsibility of the federal appeals court and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat. If the lead azide spontaneously detonates on their watch, Trump claimed, they will be fully to blame.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.

In a social media post Sunday evening, Sand called for answers on how the situation was able to become so dangerous, specifically raising the question of why MuniRem’s contract was canceled.

“Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” he wrote.

#226. Pakistani astronaut to join Chinese space mission

A Pakistani astronaut is set to become to the first foreigner to board China's Tiangong space station. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a payload specialist, will join the Shenzhou-24 mission when it launches on Wednesday.

China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for this week's Shenzhou-24 space mission, with a Pakistani payload specialist set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its Tiangong space station.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said that Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old former Pakistani air force pilot, would join two Chinese colleagues when the mission launches from the Jiuquan launch center in China's northwestern Gobi Desert at 8:18 a.m. local time (0018 GMT)  on Wednesday.

"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.

"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant milestone in relations between Islamabad and Beijing who are this year marking 75 years of cooperation in space.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the mission as a "source of joy and pride for the entire nation" and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the mission underscored the "iron brotherhood" between the two countries.

"This mission is not a finish line; I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut and one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond," said Ali.

"Together with my Chinese crew mates, I will show that this friendship is real, not only on paper, but also in orbit."

Ali will not be the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar explorer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023. But he will be the first foreign astronaut to join a Chinese mission.

During a short orbital flight expected to last around five days, Ali will carry out a series of experiments in the fields of biotechnology and photosynthetic microorganisms before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked at the Tiangong in May.

China has poured billions of dollars into its space program. Its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.

Beijing is aiming to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030 and is seen as the main space rival to the United States, which is hoping to return to the lunar surface in 2028.

#225. Why the FAA doesn't want you to put AirPods in your luggage

Air travel rules treat one part of your AirPods differently, and knowing where to pack them can save you some trouble on your next trip.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Anyone who's flown in the US is well aware of how fickle passenger rules can be. It's only in 2025 that passengers got to stop taking off their shoes during security screenings, and other rules seem to be applied inconsistently. Though some electronics are definite red flags for the TSA, it's possible that screeners at one airport could insist you take a gadget out of your bag, while the crew at another fumes at you for holding up the line. Or vice versa.

Believe it or not, AirPods are another potential point of controversy, despite them being virtually omnipresent because of the iPhone and their noise-canceling capabilities. You should actually be fine bringing them with you to watch movies or listen to podcasts. Instead, the issue is whether or not you can stash them in checked luggage.

You might think that would be an innocuous move, but the reality is the opposite, at least if you read the letter of the law. There is some justification, too: the lithium-ion battery in your AirPods' charging case could, in a worst-case scenario, catch fire in the cargo hold, where crews can't easily reach it.

According to the Transportation Security Administration, which in turn cites Federal Aviation Administration rules, the main issue is your AirPods' charging case. TSA rules bar you from checking lithium-ion batteries for a variety of electronics, including "portable rechargers and power banks," no matter if they're rated at 100Wh or less of capacity. You may also be barred from checking some other devices with built-in batteries, such as cordless curling irons and e-cigarettes. Don't expect to check your AirPods Max 2 just because it doesn't need a case.

The threat, according to the FAA, is the prospect of thermal runaway. If a lithium-ion battery overheats, takes damage or is simply exposed to water, there's a risk that it'll catch fire mid-flight, and it would be hard to tackle if it's deep within a cargo hold. Worse, lithium fires are notoriously resistant to conventional firefighting methods. Crews may need to douse the battery with water, since a conventional halon extinguisher can put out the flames but can't cool the cells enough to stop the fire from reigniting.

Is there a high chance of thermal runaway with your AirPods case? Probably not. Apple tends to maintain high manufacturing standards, and AirPods cases are durable, able to survive plenty of jolts and drops. But all it would take is one fluke to result in tragedy, which is presumably why the TSA and FAA have a strict policy regardless of brand. There's at least some chance of smothering or isolating a fire if you've got AirPods in your carry-on.

While there are too many international regulations to touch on, as far as the US goes, you should plan on bringing all of your battery devices in carry-on baggage if they're not being worn, from AirPods and power banks to your laptop. That includes anything you're taking as a gift. For personal grooming, you can save yourself a lot of trouble by putting together a completely non-electric travel kit. Hotel rooms do often include their own hair dryers, you know.

When you reach security screening, don't split hairs if you want to save time. If it's electronic, take it off your wrist, off your head or out of your pocket, and leave it loose in the provided bin(s). You should always remove laptops, tablets and e-readers from their bags and sleeves, no matter if a previous airport let you get away with keeping them in. The worst that can happen is that you'll need more bins, and that you'll take a few moments longer putting things back when screening is done.

If there's any doubt about whether a device or accessory is flight-legal, it's best to either check the TSA's website or leave it at home. In fact, you can save yourself even more trouble by reducing the number of gadgets with you to the bare minimum. You'll probably want your AirPods, but if you're already taking your phone and laptop with you, you can leave your iPad and Steam Deck behind, which will speed up screening and make packing and charging less complicated.

#224. Tidal is banning fully AI-generated music. Heres how other streaming services compare.

Music streaming services add thousands of new songs every day, and a growing share of them are made entirely with AI. Some apps have started labeling those tracks or keeping them out of recommendations.

Starting Dec. 9, Tidal will begin to remove all fully AI-generated songs from its catalog and block new uploads. Robert Andersen, who leads Tidal at parent company Block, expects about 29 million tracks to come down by the start of 2027.

"We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit. TIDAL will continue to make decisions that support real artists first," Andersen wrote in a post on X. (DSP stands for digital service provider, which is a platform that streams or sells music — like Spotify, Apple Music, or Deezer.)

Tidal started labeling tracks as "wholly" AI-generated and cutting off royalties back in July. It also moved to take down songs linked to fraud, including artist impersonation. But, according to the service, the uploads kept coming. Tidal flagged 43 percent of the tracks it received over the past 90 days as fully AI-generated, and Andersen estimates the service will turn away 80,000 to 85,000 tracks a day once the ban takes effect.

Most of those songs go unheard (thankfully). Tidal has already tagged about 27 million tracks as fully AI-generated, roughly 6.3 percent of its catalog. The company says 96 percent of those tracks went unplayed over the past three months.

Some listeners treated the ban as a reason to stick with Tidal or switch to it. "I’m genuinely so happy to have switched from Spotify to this," one commenter wrote in the subreddit, r/TIdaL. On X, another tagged Spotify and asked, "yours when?"

Other replies zeroed in on the word "wholly." One user joked that AI artists would start hiring someone "just to clap on beat." Another asked, "so 1 real cough in the intro and it’s allowed?" Behind the jokes was a practical question for Tidal: how much human input makes a recording AI-assisted?

Even some people who liked the policy wondered how Tidal would enforce it. "Fair play to Tidal, no idea how they’re going to actually catch it all though," wrote one X user. That's the challenge facing the service once it starts deciding which tracks can stay and which come down.

Apple Music is relying on labels and distributors to disclose how AI was used. Its current delivery specifications include tags for cases where AI generated a significant part of a recording, composition, music video, or artwork. A separate tag covers AI-generated artist personas that could pass for real people. In August, Apple told its music partners that the disclosures would become mandatory and that listeners would see a "Made With AI" label later in the year. (What gets labeled depends on what labels and distributors report when they submit the music.)

Deezer uses its own detection tool to label tracks that are fully AI-generated and keep them out of algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists. In July, the company also said it would take down AI tracks used to rack up fraudulent streams or left unplayed for at least six months. Other AI tracks can still turn up in searches, but Deezer says it plans to give listeners a switch to hide them by the end of the year. The company says it receives nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day.

Bandcamp put a broader ban in place in January. Its policy covers music and audio made entirely or in substantial part with generative AI, and it also prohibits the use of AI to impersonate artists or their styles.

#223. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

#222. Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic

Russian missile corvette latest casualty as Ukraine strikes back in war at sea.

Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland.

The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press. Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara.

Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli.

Casualties from the strikes included at least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, Libyan National Army officials told The Associated Press. They also mentioned some wounded crew members of the Russian warship being transferred to local hospitals.

Merkury was a Steregushchiy-class missile corvette, designated by Russia as Project 20380, that can carry both anti-ship and air-defense missiles. They are also armed with torpedoes to counter submarines and have a naval cannon mounted on the deck.

Corvette-class warships are typically smaller than the destroyers or frigates that often act as workhorses of modern navies, although NATO has designated Russian missile corvettes such as the Merkury as being equivalent to frigates.

Merkury was originally meant to join Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. But after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Russian warship was unable to enter the Black Sea because Turkey invoked the 1936 Montreux Convention to restrict warships from entering or leaving the Black Sea. Instead, the Merkury mainly operated from Russia’s Northern Fleet bases in Arctic waters, according to naval analyst HI Sutton.

The sinking of the Merkury marks the latest significant setback for the Russian Navy, which nominally remains one of the world’s leading navies in terms of number of ships and capability. The attack also shows Ukraine’s expanding geographical deployment of sea drones, which resemble low-profile drone boats that can be armed with machine guns, missiles, and explosives when engaged in kamikaze ramming missions.

Ukraine has used such drone boats in combination with flying drones and missiles to challenge the Russian Navy’s control of the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, which hold crucial shipping lanes for both countries and represent staging grounds for military operations. Ukraine has struck Russian warships at sea and in port, including another Russian missile corvette named the Boikiy that was seriously damaged by Ukrainian aerial drones while docked in St. Petersburg in June, according to Naval News.

Ukraine’s contestation of the Black Sea also undermines Russian efforts to maintain control of the Crimean Peninsula, which Russian forces seized from Ukraine in 2014. For example, Ukrainian aerial drone strikes on dozens of Russian-linked tankers and cargo ships in the Sea of Azov in July 2026 forced Russia to severely restrict resupply runs by sea.

Throughout 2026, Ukraine has also steadily increased its mid-range drone strike campaign targeting Russian roads and railways along the limited land-based supply corridors connecting Russia to Crimea.

On the nights of November 15 and November 16, waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles succeeded in collapsing one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch Strait Bridge—a structure built by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime as both a symbolic and physical link between Russia and Crimea.

That has left only the bridge’s railway still functional as a supply link for Russian-occupied Crimea, although Ukraine has continued targeting the remaining structure. Fallen debris from the bridge’s steel arch and roadway has also blocked the only deep-water route that allowed ships to pass through the Kerch Strait between the Sea of Azov and Black Sea.

But Russia has struck back with its own drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian ports and third-party ships traveling to and from Ukrainian ports. Starting in October, Russian aerial and sea drones also began striking and sinking commercial shipping near the coasts of NATO member countries Bulgaria and Romania.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has increasingly taken the fight against Russia beyond the Black Sea. Ukraine’s sinking of the Merkury and strike on the MV Angara are only the latest examples of such strikes in the Mediterranean Sea.

The most notable previous example involved the liquefied natural gas tanker Arctic Metagaz—a shadow fleet ship sanctioned for carrying Russian oil—that was wrecked by massive explosions while heading for Benghazi on March 3. Russia described the ship as having been struck by Ukrainian sea drones in the Mediterranean, although Ukraine did not publicly take credit for the attack, according to The Guardian.

More recently, Ukraine has also expanded its drone strikes northward to Russian-linked ships in the Gulf of Finland within the Baltic Sea. On November 11, Finnish authorities confirmed a strike on a Russian Navy Buyan-M class corvette named Naro-Fominsk, with Ukraine’s Security Service later claiming credit, according to BBC News. The damaged warship headed back to the Russian port of St. Petersburg.

That incident was followed by at least two drone strikes on the Russian dry cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on November 21, according to ERR News. The Sparta II is sanctioned by the United States and described by Ukraine as a Russian ship that has carried weapons and military equipment in the past.

Finnish authorities coordinated the rescue and response effort that also included Russian and Estonian ships, with the Sparta II eventually being towed by a Russian ship back to St. Petersburg, Reuters reported. But in a social media post, Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo also described the situation as follows: “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

#221. The reasons why you should never ignore your car's software updates

Hitting "remind me later" every time that pop-up appears may be keeping your car less secure.

Your car isn't just metal and moving parts anymore. Modern cars are more like "smartphones on wheels," with dozens of electronic control units running everything from the infotainment screen to the engine and the driver-assistance systems. All of that runs on software, and software has bugs. On a phone, a bug means an app crashes. On the road, it can mean a backup camera that won't turn on when you shift into reverse, or even a car that brakes when it shouldn't. That's why you should probably stop pressing "Remind me later" every time your car asks to be updated.

A software update is a new version of the code that runs on your car's computers, and it can change a lot more than the look of the touchscreen. Updates might clear up glitches, false warnings, and trouble connecting to your phone. They may patch security holes that could let someone attack a connected car. They can adjust things like engine or battery management, and they can sometimes add features. Some even change how the car drives. After Consumer Reports found braking problems with the original Tesla Model 3 in 2018, for example, Tesla sent out an update that shortened its braking distances.

Sometimes called over-the-air or "OTA" updates, revised software is also how many recalls get fixed now. When a safety defect is in the software, the automaker still has to issue a recall, but the repair can arrive as an update instead of a trip to the dealer. Ford, GM, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and others have done this. Tesla's recall of more than 2 million cars over Autopilot safety controls was fixed that way, with a free update sent wirelessly to owners.

Skipping an update means you keep the bugs it was meant to fix, and if it carries a recall fix, that fix never gets installed. Experts say the risks that come with not updating are more significant than the potential issues that come with updating. And that putting updates off can mean missing features and more trips to the dealer, which could ultimately make the car less safe.

Security patches work the same way, and they're often invisible to owners, which makes them easy to ignore. Car hacking has happened before. In 2015, hackers remotely took control of Chrysler vehicles and shut them down, and Chrysler had to recall 1.4 million cars, with the patch delivered on a USB stick. Tesla fixed a separate, similar Model S hack by sending an update to every owner over the air.

Your warranty can be at stake too. GM's 2025 and 2026 warranty booklets require owners to install over-the-air updates within 45 days of availability, and say damage that results from not installing them isn't covered. Tesla and Lucid have similar exclusions. Policies differ by brand (Nissan's 2025 booklet goes the other way and says owners don't pay for parts damaged by an update Nissan delivers), so it's worth checking your own.

Many updates arrive over the air, through the car's built-in cellular connection or a password-protected Wi-Fi network, and they usually show up as a prompt on the infotainment screen. If you've been tapping "later," look for an update option in the car's settings menu. Some automakers require a telematics subscription for over-the-air access, so owners without one, such as some Hyundai and Kia drivers, may need to visit a dealer, sometimes for a fee. Older cars without wireless connectivity can still be updated at a dealership, where a technician may reprogram a control module with diagnostic equipment.

Read the release notes before you start the update. Vague wording like "general improvements" is common, so call the manufacturer if you want details. Install when you won't need the car, with nobody inside and a strong signal or Wi-Fi. Some updates take just a few minutes while others can take up to 90, and many lock the car so you can't drive it. Electric cars may need a charged battery, and some gas cars have to stay running. If an update stalls, moving the car to get a better signal can help, and the dealer is the fallback.

#220. Istanbul 'lion hunt' ends with no big cat found after all

After a major search operation for a lion on the loose in Istanbul woodlands, Turkish authorities said "the animal was neither a lion nor any other big cat."

A large-scale search operation for a suspected lion sighted in woodland north of Istanbul has ended, with the animal in question found to be neither a lion nor any other type of big cat, according to the Istanbul governor's office.

The governor's office first issued a statement on Sunday evening saying that security cameras had captured footage of a lion on the loose in Sariyer, north of Istanbul's European side. It said "the lion has been located and the efforts to capture it were underway."

The parks authority also said in an online statement that police officers in the area had spotted "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras.

Turkish media published grainy images purportedly showing a lioness walking through a grassy area. Some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home.

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office also issued a statement saying it had launched an investigation focused on identifying the lion's owner.

After a day of searching, however, the Istanbul governor's office said "no ​concrete evidence indicating ‌the presence of a lion was found."

It said ⁠based on new footage, "it has been determined ⁠that the ​animal in the footage is neither a lion nor any other species of big cat."

The governor's office did not provide further information about what the animal seen in the footage was.

The earlier reports about a lion on the loose had sparked an outrage among activists.

Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."

"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," the organization said on X.

Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."

Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man.

Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be asked about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.

Although keeping wild animals as pets is forbidden in Turkey, the country has become a hub for the illegal wild animal trade as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.

In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered in a crate at Istanbul Airport.

#219. One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

The free, open source PhoneBox dashboard puts old Android screens back to work.

My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don’t meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you’re holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in “the drawer.”

Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed, works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading, since it is not available on the Google Play Store.

Credit: Nick Indge Credit: Nick Indge

The installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.

The first time you fire up PhoneBox, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.

Where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog—a collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets, such as RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.

I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.

Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did try were simple to modify and worked on the first try.

While I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is currently unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.

All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was new to the software.

Connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Users are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow needs your device camera to open the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.

These minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving quickly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth noting: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.

As long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find new lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.

PhoneBox took a tablet that was forgotten in a junk drawer and destined for donation and gave it a new lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, but I now have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers in your house, because this one is worthwhile.
